title: How closely did Canada’s high-oil scenario track inflation? The evidence behind Gravelle’s speech
summary: In Edmonton, Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle offered a way to read a central-bank scenario as a testable conditional forecast. In April, oil was around US$100 per barrel. The Bank’s base case assumed a decline toward US$75 by mid-2027 and a return of inflation to 2% in early 2027. Its alternative assumed that oil stayed expensive, keeping inflation near 3% for more than a year and calling for consecutive rate increases. By October, oil was still around US$100, refinery margins were elevated and domestic activity had been stronger than the Bank expected. Inflation had tracked the alternative more closely. Gravelle explained why this affected the Bank’s assessment without claiming that all assumptions in the alternative had materialized.

The chart data allow the claim to be checked. For 2026 Q2, the April inflation baseline was 2.6%, its high-oil alternative was 2.9%, and the corresponding value in the October series was 3.0%. For Q3 the three figures were 2.2%, 2.8% and 3.0%. Using the October-vintage values as the reference for those two completed quarters, the April baseline missed by an average of 0.60 percentage points in absolute terms. The alternative missed by 0.15 points. That difference of 0.45 points measures closeness across two observations. It says nothing by itself about what probability the Bank had attached to the alternative in April or how much of the inflation surprise was caused by oil.

The comparison also shows where simply substituting April’s alternative for the October baseline would have gone wrong. For 2026 Q4, the April base case had 2.2%, the April high-oil case 3.0% and the new October baseline 3.4%. For 2027 Q1 the respective figures were 2.0%, 3.1% and 3.5%. Those were future quarters when Gravelle spoke. The October forecast had moved beyond even the earlier high-oil trajectory in both quarters. Revised growth information, elevated refinery margins and changes in trade conditions all enter the narrative. This is a comparison of forecast vintages with different information sets. It cannot be treated as a controlled experiment that isolates the oil-price effect.

Gravelle used two earlier episodes to clarify the different questions a scenario can answer. At the onset of the pandemic the Bank could not construct a credible single most likely path. It instead published a range for activity. Chart 1 shows real GDP in 2020 Q2 ranging from 1,467 to 1,786 in the Bank’s chained-dollar series units. Relative to the Q1 value of 2,079 on the historical line, the two scenarios implied falls of approximately 29% and 14%. These are changes in the level, measured from the same starting value. The bounds were plausible paths through an extraordinary disruption. The chart does not assign a probability to either endpoint or to outcomes between them.

The July 2022 case asked a different question: how costly could disinflation become if price setters and wage earners changed their behaviour? In the hypothetical spiral, higher expected inflation led firms to raise prices, workers sought higher wages and firms raised prices again. More restrictive policy was needed to interrupt the process. The corresponding Chart 2 data put real GDP growth in 2023 Q1 at an annualized −1.74% under the spiral, compared with +1.65% in the base case. That is a 3.39 percentage-point gap in annualized quarterly growth, rather than a 3.39% loss in the level of output. The fact that the spiral did not occur does not invalidate the illustration. Its purpose was to show why a deterioration in expectations could make a given inflation overshoot substantially more expensive to reverse.

The speech connects those examples to market pricing. A central bank can make its policy more predictable by explaining the data it watches and what would change its view. More precise published rate guidance has a different risk. Investors might rely on the Bank’s stated path and do less independent work on incoming information. The Bank would then learn less from the prices it monitors, since those prices would increasingly reflect its own communications. Gravelle distinguished emergency guidance at the effective lower bound from routine guidance in normal conditions. The rate increase built into a high-oil scenario belongs to a conditional illustration. It is not an unconditional Governing Council pledge or a new November decision.

The historical timeline places the approach within a longer effort to make policy accountable. Inflation targeting began in 1991, the Monetary Policy Report followed in 1995, and scheduled rate decisions with releases began in 2000. The chart identifies pandemic scenarios in 2020, the wage-price example in 2022, summaries of deliberations in 2023, trade and tariff alternatives in 2025, and the high-oil scenario in 2026. The sequence changed what an observer could reasonably infer from silence or from a published hypothetical. A researcher studying communication across these regimes needs the publication type and contemporary information set alongside the date.

Gravelle also explained why the Bank does not release every internal scenario. A plausible alternative earns a place when the central forecast is unusually difficult to defend or when a material risk and the corresponding policy response are difficult to convey in words alone. Publishing too many could obscure which path the Council considers most likely. Accountability comes from making assumptions, decisions and subsequent evidence comparable against the 2% objective. Anchored expectations matter in practical terms: firms that expect inflation to come back to target have less incentive to build a permanent increase into their own prices.

questions.question: How much better did the oil alternative perform, and what would count as an honest out-of-sample test?
questions.detail: Freeze the April baseline and alternative at publication, use the same quarterly year-over-year CPI measure, then compare against first releases as each quarter arrives. The speech’s chart allows a two-quarter comparison using the October vintage, with mean absolute errors of 0.60 and 0.15 percentage points. Sampling uncertainty is large, and the conditional oil path itself changed. The Q4 2026 and later numbers in the October line were still forecasts. Treating them as realized outcomes would overstate the sample and introduce information unavailable when the speech was delivered.

questions.question: Did investors learn about the Bank’s response to oil or just receive a new oil-price assumption?
questions.detail: The April exercise supplied both a path for the shock and a description of the response if that path materialized. A market study should separate news about the oil curve, refinery margins and Canadian inflation from news about the Bank’s reaction. Compare rate-market changes around the original scenario publication, the October decision and this retrospective speech. The November appearance mainly interprets information available earlier. A yield move measured over the whole day could also incorporate international data, which is especially important when the shock itself is global.

questions.question: How should a communication score handle a simulated series of hikes?
questions.detail: Record which voice is speaking, what assumptions are required and whether the described instrument path is a decision, guidance, or an illustrative response inside a scenario. Here the consecutive increases belong to April’s hypothetical high-oil case. Gravelle’s explanation narrows uncertainty about how the Bank interprets sustained energy costs, but does not announce a further hike in November. Scoring every occurrence of a tightening verb equally would count the scenario, the historical decision and the explanation as three new policy signals.

questions.question: Can a scenario be informative even when it never occurs?
questions.detail: Use its stated purpose to select the relevant test. The pandemic range illustrates uncertainty in the level of activity without giving probability weights. The wage-price spiral illustrates the conditional output cost of a behavioural change that did not materialize. The high-oil exercise is partly verifiable because the conditioning shock later moved closer to the alternative. Ranking them all by point-forecast accuracy would confuse distinct uses. For the latter two, the ability to identify observable triggers and separate forecasts from outcomes is part of the research value.
